title: Chapter 55 — Of the Monstrous Pictures of Whales
paragraphs: Before long I will paint for you, as well as anyone can without a canvas, something like the whale's true form as it actually looks to the whaleman when the whale, in his own full body, is moored alongside the whale-ship where he can fairly be stepped on. So it may be worth first turning to those curious imaginary portraits of him which, right up to the present day, still confidently put the landsman's faith to the test. It is time to set the world straight on this point by proving all such pictures of the whale wrong.

The first source of all these pictorial delusions may lie among the oldest Hindu, Egyptian, and Greek sculptures. Ever since those inventive but unscrupulous ages, when the dolphin was portrayed on the marble panels of temples, on the pedestals of statues, and on shields, medallions, cups, and coins, wearing scales of chain-mail like Saladin's and a helmeted head like St. George's — ever since then, something of the same sort of license has held sway, not only in most popular pictures of the whale but in many scientific depictions of him too.

Now, by far the most ancient surviving portrait that in any way claims to be the whale's is to be found in the famous cave-temple of Elephanta, in India. The Brahmins maintain that in the almost endless sculptures of that immemorial temple, all the trades and pursuits, every conceivable occupation of man, were prefigured ages before any of them actually came into being. No wonder, then, that our noble profession of whaling should in some way have been foreshadowed there. The Hindu whale referred to occurs in a separate section of the wall, depicting the incarnation of Vishnu in the form of leviathan, known to scholars as the Matse Avatar. But though this sculpture is half man and half whale, so as to show only the tail of the latter, even that small section of him is all wrong. It looks more like the tapering tail of an anaconda than the broad palms of the true whale's majestic flukes.

But go to the old galleries, and look now at a great Christian painter's portrait of this fish; for he succeeds no better than the antediluvian Hindu. It is Guido's picture of Perseus rescuing Andromeda from the sea-monster or whale. Where did Guido get the model for such a strange creature as that? Nor does Hogarth, in painting the same scene in his own "Perseus Descending," make out one bit better. The huge bulk of that Hogarthian monster undulates on the surface, scarcely drawing one inch of water. It has a sort of howdah (the canopied seat carried on an elephant's back) on its back, and its gaping, tusked mouth, into which the waves are rolling, might be taken for the Traitors' Gate that leads by water from the Thames into the Tower. Then there are the Prodromus whales of old Scotch Sibbald, and Jonah's whale as depicted in the prints of old Bibles and the woodcuts of old primers. What shall be said of these? As for the bookbinder's whale winding like a vine-stalk round the stock of a descending anchor — as stamped and gilded on the spines and title-pages of many books both old and new — that is a very picturesque but purely fabulous creature, copied, I take it, from similar figures on antique vases. Though it is universally called a dolphin, I nevertheless call this bookbinder's fish an attempt at a whale, because that is what it was meant to be when the device was first introduced. It was introduced by an old Italian publisher somewhere around the 15th century, during the Revival of Learning; and in those days, and even down to a comparatively late period, dolphins were popularly supposed to be a species of the Leviathan.

In the vignettes and other ornaments of some old books you will sometimes come across very curious stabs at drawing the whale, in which all sorts of spouts, fountains, hot springs and cold, Saratoga and Baden-Baden, come bubbling up out of his never-exhausted brain. On the title-page of the first edition of the "Advancement of Learning" you will find some curious whales.

But setting aside all these amateur efforts, let us take a look at those pictures of leviathan that claim to be sober, scientific drawings by people who know. Old Harris's collection of voyages contains some plates of whales taken from a Dutch book of voyages from A.D. 1671, titled "A Whaling Voyage to Spitzbergen in the ship Jonas in the Whale, Peter Peterson of Friesland, master." One of these plates shows the whales lying among islands of ice like great rafts of logs, with white bears running across their living backs. Another plate commits the prodigious blunder of giving the whale upright flukes.

Then there is an imposing quarto by a certain Captain Colnett, a Post Captain in the English navy, titled "A Voyage round Cape Horn into the South Seas, for the purpose of extending the Spermaceti Whale Fisheries." This book contains an outline that claims to be a "Picture of a Physeter or Spermaceti whale, drawn by scale from one killed on the coast of Mexico, August, 1793, and hoisted on deck." I don't doubt the captain had this truthful picture drawn for the benefit of his marines. To mention just one thing about it: it has an eye which, enlarged by the accompanying scale to fit a full-grown sperm whale, would make that whale's eye a bow-window about five feet long. Ah, my gallant captain, why didn't you give us Jonah looking out of that eye!

Even the most conscientious compilations of Natural History written for the young and tender are not free of the same monstrous kind of error. Look at that popular work, "Goldsmith's Animated Nature." The abridged London edition of 1807 has plates of a so-called "whale" and a "narwhal." I don't want to seem crude, but this unsightly whale looks a lot like an amputated sow; and as for the narwhal, one look at it is enough to make you marvel that in this nineteenth century such a hippogriff could be passed off as genuine on any intelligent public of schoolboys.

Then again, in 1825, Bernard Germain, Count de Lacépède, a great naturalist, published a scientific, systematic book on whales, in which there are several pictures of the different species of the Leviathan. All of these are incorrect; and as for the picture of the Mysticetus or Greenland whale (that is to say, the Right whale), even Scoresby, a man of long experience with that species, declares that it has no counterpart in nature.

But the crowning touch to all this blundering was saved for the scientific Frederick Cuvier, brother of the famous Baron. In 1836 he brought out a Natural History of Whales, in which he offers what he calls a picture of the Sperm Whale. Before you show that picture to any Nantucketer, you had better plan a quick escape from Nantucket. In a word, Frederick Cuvier's Sperm Whale is not a Sperm Whale but a squash. Naturally, he never had the benefit of a whaling voyage (men like him seldom have), but where he got that picture from, who can say? Perhaps he got it the same way his scientific predecessor in the field, Desmarest, got one of his authentic abortions — from a Chinese drawing. And what lively lads with a pencil the Chinese are, plenty of odd cups and saucers can tell us.

And the sign-painters' whales you see in the streets, hanging over oil-dealers' shops — what can be said about them? They are usually Richard III whales, with dromedary humps and a very savage look, breakfasting on three or four sailor tarts — that is, whaleboats full of sailors — while their deformed bodies flounder in seas of blood and blue paint.

But these many mistakes in depicting the whale are not so very surprising after all. Consider! Most of the scientific drawings have been taken from the stranded fish; and these are about as accurate as a drawing of a wrecked ship with a broken back would be in representing the noble animal itself in all its unbattered pride of hull and spars. Though elephants have stood for their full-length portraits, the living Leviathan has never yet fairly floated himself for his. The living whale, in his full majesty and significance, is only to be seen at sea in unfathomable waters; and afloat, the vast bulk of him is out of sight, like a launched ship-of-the-line; and out of that element it is eternally impossible for mortal man to hoist him bodily into the air so as to preserve all his mighty swells and undulations. And, not to speak of the highly probable difference in outline between a young suckling whale and a full-grown Platonic Leviathan — even in the case of one of those young suckling whales hoisted to a ship's deck, his shape is then so outlandish, eel-like, limp and changeable that the devil himself could not catch his precise expression.

But you might suppose that the naked skeleton of a stranded whale would give accurate hints about his true shape. Not at all. For one of the more curious things about this Leviathan is that his skeleton tells you very little about his general form. Jeremy Bentham's skeleton, which hangs as a candelabrum in the library of one of his executors, correctly conveys the idea of a burly-browed utilitarian old gentleman, along with all of Jeremy's other leading personal traits; but nothing of the kind could be deduced from any leviathan's assembled bones. In fact, as the great anatomist Hunter says, the bare skeleton of the whale stands in the same relation to the fully clothed and padded animal as the insect does to the chrysalis that wraps it so roundly. This peculiarity shows up strikingly in the head, as will be shown in passing somewhere in this book. It also shows up very curiously in the side fin, whose bones match those of the human hand almost exactly, lacking only the thumb. This fin has four regular bone-fingers: index, middle, ring, and little finger. But all of them are permanently sealed inside their fleshy covering, the way human fingers are inside an artificial one. "However recklessly the whale may sometimes treat us," humorous Stubb said one day, "no one can truly say he handles us without mittens."

For all these reasons, then, whichever way you look at it, you are bound to conclude that the great Leviathan is the one creature in the world that must stay unpainted to the very end. True, one portrait may come much closer to the mark than another, but none can hit it with any great precision. So there is no earthly way of finding out exactly what the whale really looks like. And the only way to get even a fair idea of his living outline is to go whaling yourself; but if you do, you run no small risk of being stove in and sunk by him for good. So it seems to me you had better not be too fussy in your curiosity about this Leviathan.
